o: Air trapped under the last coat of antifouling
Galvanic corrosion eating into the laminate
Delamination of a balsa core under the skin
why: Water diffuses through the gelcoat and reacts with the resin: acid fluid in blisters below the waterline is osmosis.

o: Gelcoat crazing — fill, fair and polish the surface
Osmosis in the deck — dry it out under covers
Normal deck flex — fit a bigger backing plate
why: Water in through unsealed bolt holes rots the core and parts it from the skins; re-core and seal every hole in epoxy.

lines: Tapped round the windlass: a dull thud

o: Re-torque the keel bolts and sail as planned
Fill and fair the joint crack, then sail
Sail, and pump and check the bilge every watch
why: The moulded grid spreads the keel's loads into the hull; once it has parted, the keel is not properly held. Survey and repair first.

o: Overcoat with copper antifouling, which stops the rust
Fit an extra zinc anode inside the bilge
Wire-brush the loose rust and touch up in enamel
why: Steel rusts wherever its coating is broken: clean to bright metal, epoxy-prime and recoat; an anode in the bilge protects nothing.

o: Fine — copper is the best antifouling for any hull
Fine, as long as the zinc anodes are renewed
Copper is fine below the waterline, not above
why: Copper and aluminium make a galvanic cell: copper paint on an aluminium hull eats the hull. Use a copper-free antifouling.

Primer touched up where scratched

o: Salt damage — rinse it well with fresh water
Worm — treat with insecticide and fill it
Dried-out wood — oil it until it swells
why: Fungal rot needs fresh water and still air; salt water slows it. Cut out to sound timber, scarph in new wood, re-bed the fitting.

Condensation running down the cold hull

Tighten the starboard cap shroud to stiffen it

o: Surface rust only — tighten and paint the nuts

o: A burnt exhaust valve in cylinder 3

a: Crack the injector pipe unions and crank until fuel spurts
o: Keep cranking — it will draw the air through
Change the new filters — one must be faulty
Spray start aid into the air intake
why: Air is trapped between the injection pump and the injectors: slacken each union at the injector, crank, tighten as fuel comes.

o: It was overfilled at the last change — drain some
Coolant is getting in — the head gasket
Normal — warm oil reads higher and thinner

The raw-water seacock left partly closed

o: Parallel the batteries and crank it harder

Bleed the fuel system — it is an air lock

o: No — only 80 of the 250 hours are used
Only if the oil on the dipstick looks dark
No — it falls due at the next 250 h
why: Intervals are 'hours or months, whichever comes first': oil ages and gathers acid and moisture even while the engine sits.

q: After a diversion, fuel is short in your planing motor yacht. At which speed does she go furthest on what is left?
a: 8 kn
o: 26 kn
22 kn
30 kn
why: Litres per mile = L/h ÷ kn: 8 kn 4.5, 26 kn 9.2, 22 kn 9.5, 30 kn 10.3. Slow, off the plane and below the hump, goes furthest.
